subject: ss-medical-oncology
title: Venous access devices, infusion pumps and extravasation

steps.tx: An **implanted port** (a small reservoir placed under the skin and joined to a large central vein) gives long-term central access. A surgically placed port, often called a mediport, is reasonable only once blood cultures clearly show that the bloodstream infection has cleared. While central access is still needed during an infection, a **peripherally inserted central catheter** (PICC, a line placed without surgery) is the reasonable choice. Central lines also spare repeated venipuncture for blood draws during prolonged **myelosuppression** (low blood cell production caused by treatment).
steps.say: An implanted port is a small reservoir placed under the skin and joined to a large central vein. It gives long-term central access. A surgically placed port, often called a mediport, is reasonable only once blood cultures clearly show that the bloodstream infection has cleared. While central access is still needed during an infection, a peripherally inserted central catheter, a line placed without surgery, is the reasonable choice. Central lines also spare repeated needle sticks for blood draws during prolonged myelosuppression, which means low blood cell production caused by treatment.

rows: Reasonable while central access is still needed during infection
Used for blood draws instead of venipuncture during prolonged myelosuppression

steps.tx: **Catheter-related bloodstream infection** (an infection that travels into the blood along an indwelling line) is a major target for prevention. Prevention begins at insertion, with **aseptic technique** (methods that keep germs out of a sterile field) built into a bundle, or checklist, of evidence-based steps. Every staff contact with the catheter is a possible contamination event. These infections triple a patient's risk of in-hospital death. Daily full-body cleansing with 2% **chlorhexidine gluconate** is effective and is standard care in intensive care units (ICUs).
steps.say: Catheter-related bloodstream infection means germs travel into the blood along a line that stays in the body. It is a major target for prevention. Prevention begins at insertion, where aseptic technique keeps germs out of the sterile field. Teams follow a checklist of steps that have good evidence behind them. Each time staff touch the catheter, germs could get in. These infections triple a patient's risk of dying in hospital. Daily full-body washing with 2 percent chlorhexidine gluconate is effective, and it is standard care in intensive care units.

nodes.label: Aseptic handling at every catheter contact

steps.tx: An **infusion pump** gives a drug at a programmed rate, and battery-operated pumps of this kind are described as accurate to within 2.5 to 6%. **Midazolam**, a sedative, may run at 1 to 5 milligrams per hour. **Programmable pumps** can also add a patient-triggered dose with a **lockout interval** (the fixed wait between doses). A **smart pump** is set for each medication and dose, and it warns staff when a dose that is too high is about to be given.
steps.say: An infusion pump gives a drug at a programmed rate. Battery-operated pumps of this kind are described as accurate to within two and a half to six percent. Midazolam, a sedative, may run at one to five milligrams per hour. Programmable pumps can also give a patient-triggered dose, with a lockout interval set between doses. A smart pump is set for each medication and dose. It warns staff when a dose that is too high is about to be given.

left.title: Programmable infusion pump
points: Continuous infusions written as amount per hour
Optional patient-triggered dose with lockout interval

right.title: Smart pump safety
points: Set for each medication and dose
Warns before a too-high dose is given

steps.tx: A **vesicant** (a drug that injures tissue when it leaks out of a vein) can cause serious harm if it escapes, and that leak is called **extravasation**. **Doxorubicin** is a potent vesicant from the anthracycline group. Severe skin necrosis (tissue death) can follow a leak. It may need surgical **debridement** (cutting away dead tissue) and skin grafts. Necrosis can appear 4 to 7 days after the leak, and infusions through a central venous catheter are recommended.
steps.say: A vesicant is a drug that injures tissue when it leaks out of a vein. A leak like that is called extravasation. Doxorubicin is a potent vesicant from the anthracycline group. Severe skin necrosis, meaning tissue death, can follow a leak. It may need surgical removal of dead tissue and skin grafts. Necrosis can appear four to seven days after the leak. Infusions through a central venous catheter are recommended.

rows: Potent vesicant with severe skin necrosis
Necrosis can appear 4 to 7 days later

steps.tx: **Dexrazoxane**, an **intracellular chelating agent** (a drug that binds metal ions inside cells), can mitigate a doxorubicin leak. The first dose should start as soon as possible, within 6 hours of the leak. It is then given once daily for 3 days, at 1000 mg/m2 on day 1, 1000 mg/m2 on day 2 and 500 mg/m2 on day 3. Each infusion runs over 1 to 2 hours into a large vein away from the leak.
steps.say: Dexrazoxane is an intracellular chelating agent, meaning it binds metal ions inside cells. It can mitigate a doxorubicin leak. The first dose should start as soon as possible, within 6 hours of the leak. It is then given once a day for three days, at 1000 milligrams per square metre on day one and day two, and 500 on day three. Each infusion runs over one to two hours into a large vein away from the leak.

steps.tx: For an anthracycline leak, a **cold compress** (a cold pack held on the area) narrows local blood flow and limits how far the drug spreads. It must come off at least 15 minutes before dexrazoxane starts. If dexrazoxane is not available or is contraindicated, topical **dimethyl sulfoxide** (DMSO, a skin solvent) is the alternative, applied every 8 hours for 7 days. DMSO must not be combined with dexrazoxane.
steps.say: For an anthracycline leak, a cold compress is placed on the area. It narrows local blood flow and limits how far the drug spreads. The cold must come off at least 15 minutes before dexrazoxane starts. If dexrazoxane is not available or is contraindicated, a topical solvent called dimethyl sulfoxide is the alternative. It is applied every 8 hours for 7 days. It must never be combined with dexrazoxane.

left.title: Cold compress for anthracycline leaks
points: Limits how far the drug spreads
Removed at least 15 minutes before dexrazoxane

right.title: Topical DMSO (alternative)
points: Used if dexrazoxane is unavailable or contraindicated

steps.tx: **Vinca alkaloids** are potent vesicants too. If a leak is suspected, treatment stops and staff try to aspirate (draw out with a syringe) any drug left in the tissue. **Heat**, not ice, is then applied promptly, for one hour at a time, four times each day, for three to five days, to limit tissue damage. The vein should also be flushed after treatment to lower the risk of **phlebitis** (inflammation of the vein).
steps.say: Vinca alkaloids are potent vesicants too. If a leak is suspected, treatment stops, and staff try to draw out any drug left in the tissue. Heat, not ice, is then applied promptly, for one hour at a time, four times each day, for three to five days, to limit tissue damage. The vein should also be flushed after treatment to lower the risk of inflammation.

nodes.label: Heat, not ice: 1 hour, four times daily for 3 to 5 days

steps.tx: **Hyaluronidase**, an enzyme that loosens tissue, is injected under the skin around the vinca leak site. Six small injections go in a clockwise circle, using a 25-gauge needle that is changed for each one. The dose is 150 to 1500 units. This may ease discomfort and latent cellulitis (hidden infection of the tissue). A surgical consultation to consider early debridement is also recommended.
